lead: Frisco is one of the newest big cities in Texas, and its homes fail in newer ways: attic water heaters, PEX fittings and hail-hit roofs. DryFlare gets the water out and the drying started.
risk: attic water heater leaks, hail roof damage and freeze-burst pipes
risk_short: attic water heaters, hail, frozen pipes
why: Half of Frisco's homes were built in 2009 or later, so old pipes are rare here. The trouble sits overhead instead. Many North Texas builders put the water heater and much of the plumbing in the attic. When a tank or fitting fails up there, water runs through insulation and drywall before anyone sees it. The first sign is often a sagging ceiling in a bedroom or a stain over the garage.

Weather adds two more risks. Collin County sits in one of the busiest hail zones in the country, and new roofs crack just like old ones. The February 2021 freeze also showed how fast attic pipes can split when power drops. Frisco also sits on expansive clay, so slab plumbing takes stress as the ground swells and shrinks with the seasons.
image_alt: Ceiling drywall collapsed after a leak from above in a Frisco-area home
image_caption: In newer Frisco homes, attic leaks often show up first as a sagging ceiling.
tips: Check the drain pan under an attic water heater twice a year.
Add a leak sensor with an alarm next to the attic tank.
Insulate attic lines and open cabinet doors on hard freeze nights.
Get the roof checked after any hail, even with no leak yet.
areas: Calls come from Starwood, Stonebriar, Newman Village, Phillips Creek Ranch, Richwoods, Frisco Lakes, Panther Creek and The Trails, plus nearby Little Elm, Prosper and The Colony.

faq.q: Why do so many Frisco water leaks start in the attic?
faq.a: Many Frisco homes have the water heater, supply lines and AC drain in the attic. A failed tank, a cracked fitting or a clogged drain pan can soak insulation and ceilings below. A pan with a working drain line and a leak alarm cuts that risk.
